paper_title: Can Discrete Tokens Serve as Semantically Lossless Representations of Visual Signals?

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Discrete visual tokens represent vision in a discrete form analogous to language, offering a native interface for multimodal modeling under a shared next-token prediction objective. However, quantization error is widely assumed to cause unavoidable semantic loss, fundamentally limiting the semantic fidelity of discrete visual tokens and positioning continuous visual representations as an intrinsic upper bound. Using multimodal understanding as a proxy for semantic fidelity, we revisit this assumption and find quantization error unreliable, as discrete representations with substantially larger errors can achieve better understanding. Instead, the effective bit budget of discrete indices emerges as a key determinant of downstream performance. However, existing quantizers eventually saturate as additional codebooks contribute progressively less semantic information. As one approach to alleviating this saturation, we introduce Factorized Vector Quantization, which quantizes complementary, fixed-dimensional views of the visual feature with symmetric parallel codebooks. It continues to improve at larger bit budgets, ultimately matching continuous visual representations in multimodal understanding. Trained on industrial-scale multimodal data, our model achieves state-of-the-art performance among discrete-representation models, outperforming UniAR and Emu3-Chat by 22.8% and 59.2%, respectively, on a nine-metric average. To our knowledge, it is also the first discrete-representation model competitive with strong continuous-representation models such as Qwen3-VL, including on fine-grained OCR tasks. We further identify the key principles and a practical recipe enabling this competitiveness. These results and insights support the potential of discrete visual representations to underpin large-scale native multimodal foundation models. Code and models are available at https://github.com/hustvl/FVQ

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Recent multimodal models are moving beyond the conventional pipeline of attaching standalone vision encoder to language model through approaches such as early-fusion pretraining (Qwen Team, 2026; Kimi Team et al., 2026) and encoder-free designs (Diao et al., 2024, 2025, 2026). More ambitiously, recent work pursues the grand unification of multimodal modeling by representing images as discrete tokens analogous to text (Wang et al., 2024a; Geng et al., 2025; Meituan LongCat Team et al., 2026). By bringing vision and language under shared token interface, this formulation allows multimodal models to inherit the mature architectures, training paradigms, and scaling recipes of LLMs. Beyond serving as common modeling interface, discrete visual representations can also function as visual chains of thought (Yang et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026) or intermediate semantic representations (Wang et al., 2026), providing explicit guidance for image generation, spatial understanding, and depth estimation within unified multimodal models. However, quantizing continuous visual features into finite codebook inevitably incurs quantization error, which is widely assumed to entail semantic loss. Under this view, discrete representations cannot serve as semantically faithful proxy for the original visual signal, making continuous visual representations natural upper bound on downstream performance. 1 Figure 1 Scaling the bit budget of discrete visual representations. (a) Average multimodal understanding performance improves with the per-patch bit budget. FVQ continues to improve in the high-budget regime and reaches the continuous QwenViT baseline, whereas existing multi-codebook quantizers saturate. (b) Qualitative examples of text recognition at increasing bit budgets. Higher budgets progressively recover the fine-grained textual information required for correct predictions; green and red denote correct and incorrect answers, respectively. In this work, we challenge this common assumption. We use multimodal understanding as proxy for semantic fidelity, since representation that provides the information needed to answer any image-centric question can be regarded as semantically lossless with respect to the original visual signal (Meituan LongCat Team et al., 2026). Our experiments reveal that discrete representation with an order-of-magnitude larger quantization error can nevertheless achieve substantially better understanding performance. This result demonstrates that quantization error is not reliable measure of semantic fidelity, raising fundamental question: What determines the semantic fidelity of discrete visual representations? Returning to first principles, raw visual signals, continuous features, and discrete representations are all finite-bit encodings in digital systems, whose nominal capacities can be characterized by their bit budgets, as illustrated in Fig. 2 (right). The semantic content of raw visual signals can in principle be represented with far fewer bits owing to their high redundancy, suggesting that discrete representations may approach semantic completeness with sufficiently large bit budget. For discrete representations, the bit budget grows linearly with the number of codebooks but only logarithmically with the size of each codebook C, making multi-codebook quantization more efficient scaling strategy. To test this hypothesis, we systematically scale the bit budget and observe steady improvements in downstream multimodal understanding, as shown in Fig. 1(a). However, existing multi-codebook quantizers face scaling bottleneck as additional codebooks become less semantically informative. Residual vector quantization (RVQ) (Lee et al., 2022) assigns later codebooks to progressively smaller residuals, whereas product quantization (PQ) (Jégou et al., 2011; Ma et al., 2026a) partitions the feature into increasingly narrow channel groups. Consequently, the effective semantic capacity fails to keep pace with the nominal bit budget, limiting further scaling. The observed saturation motivates quantizer designs that continue to provide newly added codebooks with informative views as the bit budget grows. As one approach to alleviating this bottleneck, we introduce Factorized Vector Quantization (FVQ), illustrated in Fig. 3, which constructs complementary, fixed-dimensional views of the same visual feature and quantizes them with symmetric parallel codebooks. Fig. 1(a) shows that FVQ continues to improve with larger bit budgets after RVQ and PQ saturate, ultimately matching continuous visual representations in multimodal understanding. Moving beyond small-scale feasibility studies, we train our model on industrial-scale multimodal data. The resulting model achieves competitive performance with flagship multimodal models across broad suite of benchmarks, demonstrating the data scalability of discrete visual representations and supporting their potential to underpin large-scale native multimodal foundation models. Our main contributions are summarized as follows. 2 We show that quantization error does not determine semantic fidelity. Starting from the first-principles observation that digital RGB images are themselves discrete finite-bit signals, we further demonstrate that sufficiently large effective bit budget enables discrete representations to match continuous ones in downstream understanding. We introduce Factorized Vector Quantization (FVQ), which provides one approach to alleviating the high-budget saturation observed in existing multi-codebook quantizers. FVQ quantizes complementary, fixed-dimensional views of the same visual feature with symmetric parallel codebooks and sustains gains as the bit budget increases. We demonstrate the data scalability of our model through industrial-scale multimodal training, achieving state-of-the-art performance among discrete-representation models with relative improvements of 22.8% over UniAR and 59.2% over Emu3-Chat on nine-metric average. To the best of our knowledge, ours is the first discrete-representation model to achieve competitive performance against flagship continuous-representation models such as Qwen3-VL. Beyond these empirical results, we distill the key principles and practical recipe that make such competitiveness possible, further supporting the potential of discrete visual representations to underpin large-scale native multimodal foundation models.

sections.title: 2 What Determines the Semantics of Discrete Visual Representations?
sections.content: Discrete visual representations provide shared token interface for vision and language, enabling native multimodal modeling and visual chains of thought while potentially reducing modality conflicts. Their limited semantic fidelity, however, remains central bottleneck. We therefore investigate what governs the semantic fidelity of discrete visual representations. Section 2.1 tests whether quantization error necessarily implies semantic loss, and Section 2.2 examines effective bit budget and the scaling bottlenecks of existing quantizers. Fig. 2 summarizes the two analyses. sections.title: 2.1 Rethinking Quantization Error and Semantic Fidelity
sections.content: Finding 1: Quantization Error Does Not Determine Semantic Fidelity. Representations with similar errors can exhibit substantially different understanding performance, whereas those with markedly different errors can retain comparable semantic information. In this section, we challenge the common assumption that continuous visual representations form an intrinsic upper bound for their discrete counterparts. prevailing view holds that mapping continuous visual features 3 to finite codebook inevitably introduces quantization error and that this distortion necessarily entails semantic loss. Under this view, discrete representations are inherently weaker than continuous ones. However, the VLM operates on discrete indices rather than reconstructed features, so quantization error need not translate directly into reduced semantic fidelity. We compare single-codebook VQ (van den Oord et al., 2017) with eight-group RVQ and construct two partial representations by retaining alternating groups. Fig. 2 (left) highlights the odd-group comparison, while Table 1 reports feature-reconstruction MSE on the ImageNet validation set (Deng et al., 2009) alongside downstream multimodal understanding performance for all variants. The results reveal counterintuitive pattern. Although the odd-group variant omits the coarse component captured by group 0 and incurs substantially greater reconstruction error, it markedly outperforms VQ and performs comparably to the even-group variant in understanding performance. Conversely, the even-group variant exhibits reconstruction error comparable to VQ but achieves much stronger understanding. Together, these contrasting cases show that reconstruction error does not determine semantic fidelity, raising more fundamental question: what governs the semantic capacity of discrete representation?

sections.title: 2.2 Bit-Budget Scaling in Discrete Visual Representations
sections.content: Finding 2: Larger Bit Budgets Improve Semantic Capacity When Added Codes Remain Informative. Increasing the discrete bit budget improves semantic fidelity and downstream multimodal understanding, ultimately enabling discrete representations to match the understanding performance of continuous visual representations. Returning to first principles, raw visual signals, continuous features, and discrete representations are all finite-bit encodings in digital systems, and their nominal capacities can be characterized by their per-patch bit budgets (Yu et al., 2026a), as summarized in Fig. 2 (right). The semantic content of raw visual signals can in principle be represented with far fewer bits owing to their high redundancy. Accordingly, we hypothesize that increasing the discrete bit budget improves semantic fidelity, provided that the additional codes remain semantically informative. To test this hypothesis, we scale the discrete bit budget and evaluate the resulting representations on downstream multimodal understanding tasks. The discrete bit budget Bdisc = log2 grows linearly with the number of codebooks but only logarithmically with the codebook size C. Larger codebooks are more difficult to optimize and may suffer from poor utilization or codebook collapse. Keeping the codebook size fixed while increasing the number of codebooks therefore provides more efficient and tractable scaling strategy. We compare RVQ with product quantization (PQ) (Jégou et al., 2011; Ma et al., 2026a), which partitions each feature into channel groups and quantizes them in parallel. Fig. 1(a) shows that both methods improve as the bit budget increases and progressively approach the continuous representation. This trend also extends to OCR, where discrete representations often struggle because quantization can discard high-frequency details (Yu et al., 2026b). Larger budgets progressively recover the fine-grained textual information required for correct predictions, as shown in Fig. 1(b). Detailed benchmark results are reported in Table 2. Despite this trend, both RVQ and PQ saturate at high bit budgets. Increasing the number of codebooks 4 Figure 3 Overview of FVQ. During quantizer training, multiple dense projections produce complementary views of the same visual feature, which are quantized in parallel by independent codebooks. The selected codewords are combined through tight-frame synthesis for feature reconstruction. In the subsequent VLM training stage, the quantizer is frozen, and only the resulting discrete indices are mapped to newly initialized token embeddings for multimodal understanding. The nine-metric average is computed over MMMU, MathVista, MMStar, OCRBench/10, ChartQA, CharXiv-DQ, CharXiv-RQ, DocVQA, and InfoVQA. from 8 to 16 doubles the nominal bit budget but yields only marginal gains in understanding performance. We attribute this saturation to diminishing information per codebook, as later RVQ groups receive weaker residuals and PQ partitions features into increasingly narrow channel groups. The nominal capacity therefore grows without corresponding increase in effective semantic capacity, showing that additional bits help only when the added codes remain semantically informative. This observation motivates quantizer designs that continue to provide informative representations to newly added codebooks as their number grows. In the next section, we introduce FVQ as one such approach.

sections.title: 3.1 Overview
sections.content: The preceding analysis shows that larger nominal bit budget is insufficient when the information available to each codebook diminishes as their number grows. scalable multi-codebook quantizer should therefore assign symmetric roles to its codebooks, provide each with fixed-dimensional view derived from the full feature, and collectively preserve the original feature before quantization. Guided by these principles, we introduce Factorized Vector Quantization (FVQ) as concrete realization based on dense tight-frame projections, parallel independent codebooks, and information-preserving synthesis, as illustrated in Fig. 3.

sections.title: 4.1 Implementation Details
sections.content: We report two training configurations: an industrial-scale configuration for the main experiments and shared configuration based primarily on the LLaVA-OneVision data (Li et al., 2024) for the exploratory experiments in Section 2 and the ablation studies. 6 Model Architecture. Our main model pairs Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025) with an any-resolution visual tokenizer constructed by applying 16-codebook FVQ to Qwen3 ViT (Bai et al., 2025a). To preserve native next-token prediction setup with minimal modality-specific modifications to the LLM, we use standard 1D RoPE (Su et al., 2024) in the LLM and omit the DeepStack connections from Qwen3 ViT. Unless otherwise specified, the exploratory and ablation experiments use Qwen3-1.7B and vary the quantization configuration according to the experiment. Training Schedule. Both configurations follow four stages. Quantizer training learns the visual tokenizer by reconstructing frozen visual features. Alignment stage freezes both the tokenizer and the LLM and optimizes the newly initialized visual token embeddings and merger to align the discrete IDs with the language embedding space. Pre-training and supervised fine-tuning both keep the tokenizer frozen and jointly optimize the LLM, visual token embeddings, and merger, using context lengths of 8K and 16K and maximum image resolutions of 1024px and 2048px, respectively. Training Data. For the main experiments, quantizer training, alignment, pre-training, and supervised fine-tuning use 100B, 10B, 60B, and 30B tokens, respectively, drawn from mixtures covering STEM, OCR, interleaved image-text sequences, image captioning and text-only data. For the exploratory and ablation experiments, we train the quantizer on 50B tokens, use approximately 4B tokens for alignment, and adopt LLaVA-OneVision (Li et al., 2024) for pre-training and supervised fine-tuning. Evaluation. We evaluate general perception and reasoning on MMMU (Yue et al., 2024), its more challenging and robust extension MMMU-Pro (Yue et al., 2025), MMStar (Chen et al., 2024a), and RealWorldQA (xAI, 2024). We assess mathematical reasoning on MathVista (Lu et al., 2024). For text recognition and text-centric understanding, we use OCRBench (Liu et al., 2024), OCRBench V2 (Fu et al., 2026), and TextVQA (Singh et al., 2019); for document and infographic understanding, we use DocVQA (Mathew et al., 2021), InfoVQA (Mathew et al., 2022), and OmniDocBench (Ouyang et al., 2025), which evaluates document parsing across diverse PDF document types. We assess diagram and chart understanding on AI2D (Kembhavi et al., 2016) with mask, ChartQA (Masry et al., 2022), and CharXiv (Wang et al., 2024b).

sections.title: 4.2 Main Results
sections.content: Bit-Budget Scaling. We compare discrete quantizers with the original continuous Qwen3 ViT representation under identical VLM training and evaluation settings. Table 2 reports the complete benchmark results underlying the scaling trend in Fig. 1(a). Increasing the number of codebooks substantially improves RVQ and PQ over single-codebook methods, but their gains diminish at high budgets. FVQ, by contrast, continues to improve with larger budgets and ultimately matches the average understanding performance of continuous QwenViT. STEM & General. Table 3 shows that our model achieves state-of-the-art performance among discreterepresentation models while remaining competitive with strong continuous-representation models. It matches Qwen3-VL-8B on MathVista and achieves the best RealWorldQA result, demonstrating that discrete visual representations can support strong reasoning and general understanding under industrial-scale training. OCR & Doc & Chart. Quantization is commonly thought to discard the high-frequency details required for OCR, document, and chart understanding, causing discrete-representation models to lag substantially behind continuous-representation models (Yu et al., 2026b). Table 4 shows that our model substantially narrows this gap, achieving state-of-the-art performance among discrete-representation models, performing comparably to Qwen3-VL-8B on OmniDocBench and DocVQA, and surpassing the continuous-representation models on both CharXiv tasks. These results suggest that weak fine-grained visual understanding is not intrinsic to discretization but instead reflects the information bottleneck imposed by an insufficient effective bit budget. sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We revisit the semantic fidelity of discrete visual tokens and show that feature reconstruction error does not reliably predict downstream understanding. Instead, effective bit budget emerges as key determinant of semantic capacity. However, existing multi-codebook quantizers eventually saturate as additional codebooks contribute diminishing semantic information. As one approach to alleviating this bottleneck, FVQ combines complementary projections with symmetric parallel codebooks and sustains gains at larger bit budgets. Moving beyond small-scale feasibility studies, our industrial-scale model achieves state-of-the-art performance among discrete-representation models and remains competitive with strong continuous-representation models, including on fine-grained OCR and document understanding. These results support discrete tokens as scalable interface for large-scale native multimodal foundation models.

sections.title: B Related Work
sections.content: B.1 Native and Unified Multimodal Modeling Multimodal foundation models are moving beyond the conventional paradigm of attaching vision encoder and lightweight adapter to pretrained language model. Recent work pursues more native multimodal modeling along two complementary directions. The first adopts early-fusion pretraining, introducing multimodal data from the outset of language-model pretraining, as exemplified by Qwen3.5 (Qwen Team, 2026) and Kimi K3 (Kimi Team et al., 2026). The second integrates visual processing directly into the multimodal backbone, reducing the architectural separation between vision and language. EVE (Diao et al., 2024), EVEv2 (Diao et al., 2025), Mono-InternVL (Luo et al., 2025), and SenseNova-U1 (Diao et al., 2026) pursue encoderfree or monolithic designs, while TML-Interaction (Thinking Machines Lab, 2026) combines encoder-free processing with early-fusion pretraining for real-time multimodal interaction. These approaches pursue native multimodality by changing when multimodal learning begins or where visual processing occurs. complementary line of work pursues unification at the representation level. Chameleon (Chameleon Team, 2024) and Emu3 (Wang et al., 2024a) represent images as discrete tokens and model vision and 17 language under shared autoregressive objective. X-Omni (Geng et al., 2025) uses shared semantic image-token space for understanding and generation, with diffusion decoder translating predicted tokens into images. LongCat-Next (Meituan LongCat Team et al., 2026) lexicalizes arbitrary-resolution visual inputs through hierarchical discrete codes, while UniAR (Peng et al., 2026) uses shared visual tokenizer to connect multimodal understanding and generation. Beyond unifying understanding and generation, visual representations can also serve as intermediate computational states. Representation Forcing autoregressively predicts visual representations before pixels and retains them in context to guide pixel-space diffusion (Wang et al., 2026). Context Unrolling enables explicit reasoning across multiple modal representations before producing predictions (Yang et al., 2026). VoT generates discrete visual-plan tokens, such as objects and layouts, to bridge high-level semantics and pixel rendering (Sun et al., 2026). Together, these works establish discrete visual tokens as promising interface for native and unified multimodal models (Zhou et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025; Zou et al., 2025). Complementary work improves multimodal understanding through generative imagination for humanobject interaction (Yuan et al., 2026b) and tool-assisted action recognition (Yuan et al., 2026a). Our work addresses the representation bottleneck underlying this interface by studying what determines the semantic fidelity of discrete visual tokens and how that capacity can be scaled. B.2 Semantic Visual Representations and Tokenization Pretrained vision-language encoders provide the semantic feature spaces that modern visual tokenizers seek to discretize. CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) learns transferable visual representations through contrastive language supervision, while SigLIP (Zhai et al., 2023) improves the scalability of image-text alignment through pairwise sigmoid objective. SigLIP2 (Tschannen et al., 2025) further strengthens semantic understanding, localization, and dense visual features. More recent VLM-oriented vision encoders, including Qwen3 ViT (Bai et al., 2025a), MoonViT-v2 (Kimi Team et al., 2026), and InternViT (Zhu et al., 2025a), are trained on large-scale task-oriented multimodal data covering OCR, document understanding, and visual question answering. Compared with CLIP-style image-text alignment, this richer supervision yields more fine-grained visual representations that better preserve textual, spatial, and structural information. These semantically structured continuous features provide natural target space for visual tokenization. RAE (Zheng et al., 2026) uses pretrained VFM features directly as continuous latents, demonstrating their suitability for reconstruction and generation. UniTok (Ma et al., 2026a) combines reconstruction with semantic supervision to support both understanding and generation. ViQ (Yu et al., 2026b) introduces text-aligned, position-aware quantization, while dRAE (Ma et al., 2026b) uses hyperspherical codes that better match the geometry of pretrained features. Despite these advances, discrete visual representations continue to lag substantially behind continuous visual representations in multimodal understanding. This persistent gap motivates us to study what governs the semantic information retained when continuous features are mapped to finite discrete indices. We isolate this process within frozen VFM feature space and use downstream multimodal understanding to evaluate the resulting representations. Our analysis shifts attention from reconstruction quality alone to the semantic information carried by discrete indices. B.3 Quantized Visual Encoders Vector quantization maps continuous features to entries in finite codebook (van den Oord et al., 2017). Recent methods improve the optimization and utilization of this discrete space from different perspectives. FSQ (Mentzer et al., 2024), LFQ (Yu et al., 2024), and BSQ (Zhao et al., 2025) replace unconstrained learned codebooks with structured scalar or binary codes, while SimVQ (Zhu et al., 2025b) and IBQ (Shi et al., 2025) improve the learning and utilization of explicit codebooks. complementary line of work expands representation capacity through multiple codebooks. Residual vector quantization recursively encodes the residual left by preceding codebooks (Lee et al., 2022), while product quantization partitions each feature into independent channel groups, as adopted by UniTok for visual generation and understanding (Jégou et al., 2011; Ma et al., 2026a). However, their gains can saturate as the 18 number of codebooks grows. Our work studies this limitation in semantic visual representations and presents FVQ as one approach to sustaining scaling through fixed-dimensional full-feature views and symmetric parallel codebooks.

sections.title: C Additional Experiments
sections.content: C.1 Additional Experimental Details Our model follows four sequential stages: tokenizer training, alignment, pre-training (PT), and supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Tokenizer training initializes from Qwen3-VL-8B ViT and optimizes the input projection, codebooks, and feature decoder while keeping the tight-frame projections fixed, reconstructing frozen visual features for 100B tokens. Alignment freezes both the tokenizer and the LLM and trains the visual token embeddings and merger for 10B tokens. PT then unfreezes the LLM and jointly optimizes it with the visual interface for 60B tokens while keeping the tokenizer frozen. SFT continues to optimize the LLM and visual interface for 30B tokens with the tokenizer frozen. All four stages use AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017) with β1 = 0.9 and β2 = 0.96.
